sentences.text:
The claim for compensation raised in this claim petition is in respect of fatal injuries alleged to have been suffered by the deceased Sh. Sikander in a road accident that took place on 12.11.2016 at about 8:00 p.m., Near Village Ludana, District Jind, Haryana, regarding which one FIR bearing No.291/2016, under Sections 279/304-A IPC was registered at PS Pillu Khera, District-Jind,
Haryana.

The vehicle involved in this case is a car bearing registration No. HR-31-L4659, which at the relevant time of accident was being owned and driven by respondent No.1 (R-1) and insured with respondent No. 2 (R-2).
2. Succinctly put, facts of case as per claim petition are that the petitioners are parents of the deceased.
On the above said date and time, the deceased along with his friend Ankit was going on a motorcycle bearing registration No. HR-20U-0493.

When they reached near Village Ludana at about 8:00 p.m., the offending vehicle bearing registration No. HR-31L-4659, which was being driven by respondent no. 1 in rash and negligent manner and in contravention of traffic rules, had hit the motorcycle with great force due to which the deceased sustained fatal injuries.
His postmortem was conducted by the doctors of Government Hospital.
3. Written statement has been filed on behalf of respondent No. 1 stating that he has been falsely implicated in the present matter to grab the compensation.

It is further stated that he was holding a valid and effective driving license and the vehicle in question was duly insured with respondent No.2/Insurance Company at the relevant time of accident.
4. Respondent no. 2/Insurance Company has filed its written statement to the claim petition stating that no accident had occurred by the alleged car and the same has been planted by the police in connivance with the petitioners as the brother of the deceased mentioned in the FIR that unknown vehicle had hit the vehicle of the deceased.
It is further stated that the present matter is a hit and run case as the driver of the alleged vehicle was arrested after 45 days of the accident.

It is further stated that the deceased was also negligent as he was not wearing helmet and not stopping co-passenger Ankit to drive in rash and negligent manner who was not following traffic rules and hence, this is a case of contributory negligence.
5.

It is pertinent to mention that the two connected claim petitions bearing MACP Nos. 39/17 &
40/17 were filed before this Tribunal arising out of the same accident and hence, vide order dated 09.05.2017, they were consolidated for the purposes of trial and decision and MACP No. 39/17 was directed to be treated as the lead case for recording of evidence.

On the same day, following consolidated issues were framed by the Ld. Predecessor of this Court as:-
1.

Whether Sh. Ankit (deceased in MACP No. 39/17) and Sh. Sikander (deceased in MACP No. 40/17) sustained fatal injuries in the accident which occurred on 12.11.2016 at about 8 PM Near Village Ludana, District Jind, Haryana caused by rash and negligent driving of vehicle No. HR-31L-4659 driven and owned by respondent No. 1 and insured with respondent No. 2?

OPP. 
2. Whether the petitioners are entitled to compensation? If so, to what amount and from whom?

sentences.text: The Tribunal heard arguments advanced by Sh. Gaurav Sood, Ld. Counsel for the petitioners and Sh. Kumar Alok, Ld. Counsel for respondent No.2/Insurance Company, as none has been appearing on behalf of R-1 since long and has perused the entire case record, along with written submissions filed on behalf of petitioners and Insurance Company.
The finding on the aforesaid issues is reproduced in succeeding paragraphs hereinafter.

1. Whether Sh. Ankit (deceased in MACP No. 39/17) and Sh. Sikander (deceased in MACP No.
40/17) sustained fatal injuries in the accident which occurred on 12.11.2016 at about 8 PM Near Village Ludana, District Jind, Haryana caused by rash and negligent driving of vehicle No.
HR-31L-4659
driven
and owned by respondent No. 1 and insured with respondent No. 2
? OPP.
7. Onus to prove this issue was upon the petitioners.
The first question that needs to be decided is whether the accident was caused by vehicle bearing registration No. HR-31L- 4659.

In order to prove the same, the petitioners have examined Sh. Satender, an eye witness to the accident as PW5 who tendered his evidence by way of affidavit as Ex. PW5/A wherein he has deposed that on 12.11.2016, he was going from Gohana to Jind, Haryana on his motorcycle and when he reached at about half km far to reach village Ludana police chowki, Haryana, he saw that a car bearing registration No. HR-31L-4659 being driven by its driver in rash and negligent manner, came from front and hit the motorcycle, which was moving in normal speed just some distance ahead of his motorcycle.
During cross examination, he deposed that the offending vehicle white colour Swift Desire had hit the motorcycle from driver side.
He further deposed that he had not given any statement to the police and the police never called him to record his statement.
He further deposed that he did not call the police as he was not carrying mobile phone at that time.

8. Petitioners have also examined ASI Mahender as PW3 who has brought the original FIR dated 13.11.2016 and deposed that after receiving a telephonic call regarding the accident, he went to the spot of accident and found that two people were injured and lying on the road.
He further deposed that they both were removed to government hospital, Jind from where they were referred to PGI Rohtak and subsequently, they expired.
One DD was registered at PS on receiving intimation in this regard.
Thereafter, on the next morning, he along with HC Wazir reached at PGI Rohtak and collected two separate rukkas regarding the death of two persons namely Ankit and Sikander from PS PGI Rohtak.
He also recorded the statement of Sh. Amandeep, brother of deceased Ankit, who was also an eye witness of the accident.

He admitted that the certified copies of documents of the criminal case record was prepared by him which have been proved as Ex. PW3/A (colly).
9.
During cross examination, he admitted that he is not an eye witness of the accident.

He deposed that the number of offending vehicle was not disclosed by the witness Amandeep Singh in his statement dated 13.11.2016, but the same was disclosed in his supplementary statement recorded on 20.12.2016, copy of which is Ex. PW3/DA.
He admitted that the witness Sh. Amandeep has not claimed himself to be an eye witness of the accident in his supplementary statement.

sentences.text: In the case of Supdt. of Police, CBI v. Tapan Kumar Singh, (2003) 6 SCC 175 and in the case of State of U.P. v. Naresh, (2011) 4 SCC 324, it is observed and held by this Court that FIR is not an encyclopaedia, which must disclose all facts and details relating to the offence reported.

entities.text: Supdt. of Police, CBI v. Tapan Kumar Singh, (2003) 6 SCC 175
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: State of U.P. v. Naresh, (2011) 4 SCC 324
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In paragraph 20 in the case of Tapan Kumar Singh (supra), it is observed and held as under:
20.
It is well settled that a first information report is not an encyclopaedia, which must disclose all facts and details relating to the offence reported.
An informant may lodge a report about the commission of an offence though he may not know the name of the victim or his assailant.
He may not even know how the occurrence took place.
A first informant need not necessarily be an eyewitness so as to be able to disclose in great detail all aspects of the offence committed.

What is of significance is that the information given must disclose the commission of a cognizable offence and the information so lodged must provide a basis for the police officer to suspect the commission of a cognizable offence.

At this stage it is enough if the police officer on the basis of the information given suspects the commission of a cognizable offence,
and not that he must be convinced or satisfied that a cognizable offence has been committed.
If he has reasons to suspect, on the basis of information received, that a cognizable offence may have been committed, he is bound to record the information and conduct an investigation.
At this stage it is also not necessary for him to satisfy himself about the truthfulness of the information.
It is only after a complete investigation that he may be able to report on the truthfulness or otherwise of the information.
Similarly, even if the information does not furnish all the details he must find out those details in the course of investigation and collect all the necessary evidence.

The information given disclosing the commission of a cognizable offence only sets in motion the investigative machinery, with a view to collect all necessary evidence, and thereafter to take action in accordance with law.

The true test is whether the information furnished provides a reason to suspect the commission of an offence, which the police officer concerned is empowered under Section 156 of the Code to investigate.
If it does, he has no option but to record the information and proceed to investigate the case either himself or depute any other competent officer to conduct the investigation.

The question as to whether the report is true, whether it discloses full details regarding the manner of occurrence, whether the accused is named, and whether there is sufficient evidence to support the allegations are all matters which are alien to the consideration of the question whether the report discloses the commission of a cognizable offence.

Even if the information does not give full details regarding these matters, the investigating officer is not absolved of his duty to investigate the case and discover the true facts, if he can."

sentences.text: Further, as per chargesheet, due investigation was conducted wherein mechanical inspection of the offending vehicle was carried out which has shown damage to the offending vehicle.

12. Respondent no. 1 has examined himself as R1W1 who tendered his evidence by way of affidavit Ex. R1W1/A and relied upon copy of his driving license as Ex. R1W1/2, attested copy of his RC as Ex.
R1W1/3 and attested copy of insurance policy as Ex. R1W1/4 wherein he has only stated that he was not driving the offending vehicle rashly and negligently.
However, he has not stated or taken a plea of alibi in his testimony.
He has also failed to explain the damage caused to his car found in the mechanical inspection report.
During cross examination, he deposed that his car, driving license and RC were impounded by the police officials of PS Pillu Khera in connection with the accident of this case.
He further deposed that a criminal case was registered against him and he was facing trial.
He volunteered that he stood acquitted in the criminal case.
He further deposed that he did not make any complaint to the police or any other authority in writing regarding false implication in the present matter.

13. Further, it has not been disputed that respondent No.1 has been charge-sheeted in the aforesaid FIR for offences punishable under Sections 279/304-A IPC for rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors.,
2018 Law Suit (SC) 303

entities.text:
Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors.,
2018 Law Suit (SC) 303
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: has observed that filing of charge sheet against the driver prima facie points towards his complicity in driving the vehicle rashly and negligently.

It has been further observed that even when the accused were to be acquitted in the criminal case, the same may be of no effect on the assessment of the liability required in respect of motor accident cases by the Tribunal.

14. As per certified copy of judgment, the respondent no. 1 was acquitted only on the basis that the prosecution failed to bring witnesses sufficient to prove on record the guilt of R-1 beyond reasonable doubt and there is no finding on the point that R-1 was not driving the offending vehicle at/near the spot of accident or his car was not involved, pointing towards the fact that the offending vehicle has been planted.

15. It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an Accident Tribunal is similar to that followed by a Civil Court and in civil matters, the facts are required to be established on preponderance of probabilities and not beyond reasonable doubt, as are required in a criminal prosecution.

Reference in this regard is made to the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court reported as (2009) 13 SC 530 in case titled as Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, wherein it has been observed that strict proof of an accident caused by a particular vehicle in a particular manner may not be possible to be done by the petitioners and the claimants were merely to establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability.

sentences.text: 16. In view of foregoing discussion, it is held that oral evidence led on record by the petitioners on this issue is duly substantiated by the documentary evidence i.e. chargesheet, and thus, it stands proved on preponderance of probabilities that the aforesaid accident took place due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle bearing No. HR-31-L4659 which was being driven and owned by respondent No. 1 and insured by respondent No. 2 at the relevant time of accident.

Hence,
this issue is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.

sentences.text: Whether the petitioners are entitled for compensation?

If so, to what amount and from whom?
17.

As rashness and negligence on part of driver of the offending vehicle/respondent No. 1 has been proved, the petitioners have become entitled to be compensation for death of their family member in the said accident, but the computation of compensation and liability to pay the same are required to be decided.
The compensation to which the petitioners are entitled shall be under the heads as discussed hereinafter.
(i) Loss of dependency 18.

The petitioner No. 1 Sh. Satya Vir Singh being father of the deceased has stepped into the witness box as PW4 and filed his evidence by way of affidavit as Ex. PW4/A wherein he has claimed that his deceased son was matriculate and was doing private service as a salesman at Mr. Foody Point, shop No. 46, Chandigarh and was getting salary of Rs. 12,000/- per month.

During cross examination, he admitted that he has not filed any document to show that her deceased son was doing private service as a salesman at Mr. Foody Point, Chandigarh and was getting salary of Rs. 12,000/- per month.

He has tendered on record copy of 10th class certificate and marksheet of his deceased son as Ex.
PW4/2 and Ex. PW4/3 respectively.

19. Since the employment and salary of the deceased has not been established on record, the minimum wages of unskilled person is taken into account as per rates prevalent in Chandigarh,
which were Rs. 325/- per day at the time of accident.

Hence, the monthly income of deceased comes out to be Rs. 8,450/- (Rs. 325 X 26 days).
20.

PW1 has stated in his affidavit that the deceased was 27 Years old at the time of accident and in order to ascertain the age of the deceased, PW1 has placed on record 10th class certificate and marksheet of his deceased son as Ex. PW4/2 and Ex. PW4/3 respectively in which the date of birth of deceased is found recorded as 01.07.1989.
Hence, going by these documents, the age of deceased at the time of accident i.e. 12.11.2016 was about 27 years, 4 months and 11 days.

In terms of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sarla Verma & Ors. Vs. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr., (2009) 6 SCC 121, which has also been approved by the Constitution Bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of National Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors.,
(2017) 16 SCC 680, the multiplier of '17' is applicable in the present case.

LIABILITY 38.

Ld. Counsel for Respondent No. 3/Insurance Company in its written submissions has stated that the deceased was not having a valid driving license and they both were not wearing helmet at the relevant time of accident, and thus, the petitioners are not entitled to claim compensation.
He has placed reliance upon the judgment of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in MAC. APP. 954/2017 & CM APPL. 39162/2017 titled as Rehmani Begum and ors Vs. Krishan Pal and ors, decided on 18.01.2019

sentences.text: wherein it has been held that if a person drives on public road without valid driving license, the act of driving was on his own risk and incase of accident, such act would not attract tortious liability.

However, the Hon'ble Apex Court in 2019 ACJ 42, Saraswati Palariya and ors Vs New India Insurance Company Ltd. and ors has held that driving without a driving license may expose the person to other liabilities but no inference of contributory negligence can be drawn on that basis.

Counsel for the insurance company that contributory negligence be fastened upon the petitioners as the deceased was not holding the driving license and was not wearing helmet at the time of accident.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In the case of Supdt. of Police, CBI v. Tapan Kumar Singh, (2003) 6 SCC 175 and in the case of State of U.P. v. Naresh, (2011) 4 SCC 324, it is observed and held by this Court that FIR is not an encyclopaedia, which must disclose all facts and details relating to the offence reported.
It is well settled that a first information report is not an encyclopaedia, which must disclose all facts and details relating to the offence reported.
An informant may lodge a report about the commission of an offence though he may not know the name of the victim or his assailant.
He may not even know how the occurrence took place.
A first informant need not necessarily be an eyewitness so as to be able to disclose in great detail all aspects of the offence committed.
What is of significance is that the information given must disclose the commission of a cognizable offence and the information so lodged must provide a basis for the police officer to suspect the commission of a cognizable offence.
At this stage it is enough if the police officer on the basis of the information given suspects the commission of a cognizable offence,
and not that he must be convinced or satisfied that a cognizable offence has been committed.
If he has reasons to suspect, on the basis of information received, that a cognizable offence may have been committed, he is bound to record the information and conduct an investigation.
At this stage it is also not necessary for him to satisfy himself about the truthfulness of the information.
It is only after a complete investigation that he may be able to report on the truthfulness or otherwise of the information.
Similarly, even if the information does not furnish all the details he must find out those details in the course of investigation and collect all the necessary evidence.
The information given disclosing the commission of a cognizable offence only sets in motion the investigative machinery, with a view to collect all necessary evidence, and thereafter to take action in accordance with law.
The true test is whether the information furnished provides a reason to suspect the commission of an offence, which the police officer concerned is empowered under Section 156 of the Code to investigate.
If it does, he has no option but to record the information and proceed to investigate the case either himself or depute any other competent officer to conduct the investigation.

It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an Accident Tribunal is similar to that followed by a Civil Court and in civil matters, the facts are required to be established on preponderance of probabilities and not beyond reasonable doubt, as are required in a criminal prosecution.
As rashness and negligence on part of driver of the offending vehicle/respondent No. 1 has been proved, the petitioners have become entitled to be compensation for death of their family member in the said accident, but the computation of compensation and liability to pay the same are required to be decided.
In terms of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sarla Verma & Ors. Vs. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr., (2009) 6 SCC 121, which has also been approved by the Constitution Bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of National Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors.,
(2017) 16 SCC 680, the multiplier of '17' is applicable in the present case.
In terms of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sarla Verma & Ors. Vs. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (Supra) and National Insurance Company Ltd. Vs.
Pranay Sethi & Ors. (Supra), 50% of earnings of deceased shall be deducted towards his personal and living expenses.
He has placed reliance upon the judgment of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in MAC. APP. 954/2017 & CM APPL. 39162/2017 titled as Rehmani Begum and ors Vs. Krishan Pal and ors, decided on 18.01.2019
wherein it has been held that if a person drives on public road without valid driving license, the act of driving was on his own risk and incase of accident, such act would not attract tortious liability.
However, the Hon'ble Apex Court in 2019 ACJ 42, Saraswati Palariya and ors Vs New India Insurance Company Ltd. and ors has held that driving without a driving license may expose the person to other liabilities but no inference of contributory negligence can be drawn on that basis.
